extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers in public administration and political science
extracted.subtask_description: A classical treatise analyzing the distinction and relationship between politics (expression of state will) and administration (execution of state will), offering principles and prescriptive reforms for organizing government, parties, and administrative systems in modern states (especially the United States and England).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider extra-legal institutions in describing government
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal governmental system (positive law, constitution) often differs from the actual political system; extra-legal institutions like parties and customs must be accounted for to understand real political life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confine study to written constitutions; analyze political customs and party systems (example: method of electing the U.S. President is governed by parties more than the Constitution). The administrative system and extra-legal forces can amend or supplement constitutional provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between expression and execution of the state will
rubrics_metrics.description: Political functions group under two heads: operations necessary to the expression (making) of the state's will (politics) and operations necessary to the execution (enforcement) of that will (administration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating governmental structures, explicitly separate organs primarily concerned with formulating state will from those primarily concerned with executing it; recognize overlapping and delegation (legislature, executive, administrative authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of harmony between making and enforcement of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal formulation and actual enforcement must be in accord; executing authority must be subordinated to the law-making authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether mechanisms exist to ensure execution conforms to legislative intent; consider how misalignment leads to ineffective government and extra-legal political control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers is a useful principle but legally unworkable in absolute form
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu's tripartite separation (legislative, executive, judicial) underpins theory, but in practice authorities overlap and exceptions are frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept separation as analytic ideal; in evaluation, look for 'vicinage' and tolerated encroachments; analyze constitutional provisions and judicial exceptions rather than expecting absolute separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate primary from secondary governmental functions
rubrics_metrics.description: As systems develop, the two primary functions (expression and execution) subdivide into many minor/secondary functions each entrusted to specific organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map which organs perform which minor functions (e.g., constitution-making vs. ordinary legislation; judicial application vs. administrative technical tasks) when assessing institutional design and competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political control should extend to execution of law but not to technical administrative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Political oversight is proper for executing state will (to make executing authorities accountable), but should not be extended to the detailed, technical, quasi-judicial, or scientific parts of administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scope of political authority: permit control over law enforcement and policy direction, but protect administrative decisions that require technical expertise; identify evils where political control intrudes into technical administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper extent of political control over administration
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a proper extent to which politics may control administration; too great an extent produces evils (corruption, inefficiency), while too little undermines responsiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether political control balances accountability and administrative efficiency; identify signs of overreach (spoils, patronage) and under-control (unresponsive bureaucracies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of judicial authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial authorities should be independent and immune from political control in order to fairly apply law in concrete controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for tenure protections, removal safeguards, and institutional arrangements (e.g., Act of Settlement) that secure judicial independence; consider effect of judicial decisions on separation of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of local administrative authorities (local self-government)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local administrative autonomy affects enforcement and the character of politics; localities as 'states in miniature' need meaningful powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree of local autonomy (general/local powers, charter rights, control by central administration); weigh advantages of local self-government versus centralization for enforcement, responsiveness, and corruption control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of administration as remedy for fragmented state administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater centralization of state administrative systems (following national model) can prevent numerous administrative authorities from obstructing state law execution and thereby allow depoliticization of administrative offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider centralization to reduce multiplicity of authorities; but also examine potential dangers of centralization (over-concentration, loss of local responsiveness); assess readiness for accompanying safeguards (civil service reform).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative officers should be made permanent (civil service) though permanence has tensions with popular government
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanence of administrative officers (merit-based tenure) increases administrative efficiency and removes administrative offices from politics, but permanence can conflict with principles of popular control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tenure systems: adopt competitive examinations and protections for administrative tenure to secure expertise, while designing accountability mechanisms so permanence does not negate democratic responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralized administrative systems make administrative officers political
rubrics_metrics.description: Where administration is decentralized without central supervision, local administrative officers become partisan/political actors (leading to spoils and patronage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether administrative decentralization is accompanied by political appointments and local party-machine control; if so, expect politicization of administration and consider centralization or professionalization remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative control often fails to supervise administration effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures may lack the apparatus or political will to supervise execution, yielding to party control or to administrative autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legislative competence and capacity for oversight; look for examples of failure (e.g., prohibition enforcement), and consider strengthening central supervision or administrative institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoils/rotation in office produces administrative inefficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotation and spoils systems lead to incompetence and politicized administration; the spoils system arose from a combination of decentralized administration and party control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical analysis to identify origin and effects of spoils; recommend competitive examinations and centralization as antecedents to civil service reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Service Reform is linked to centralization of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil service reform historically followed or accompanied centralization of administration; centralization made it possible to take administration out of politics and institute merit systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning reforms, pair structural centralization with merit-based personnel systems (competitive exams, fixed tenure) to depoliticize appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong parties are necessary for popular government where administration is decentralized
rubrics_metrics.description: The work parties must do is greater where administration is decentralized; strong parties can be necessary to coordinate and make government work, though they risk excess control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate party strength relative to administrative structure: decentralization requires strong parties, but ensure checks to prevent party abuses and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of too-extended political control (bosses and corruption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive party control produces 'boss' systems with concentrated, often irresponsible power that undermine deliberative legislatures and popular responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify boss-like actors, concentration of appointment powers, erosion of legislative deliberation; consider reforms to make bosses/parties responsible (party accountability, legal recognition with public control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make parties legally recognized but subject to effective public control
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal recognition of political parties alone is insufficient; parties as legally recognized political organs should be subjected to public control to increase their responsiveness and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design party laws that combine recognition with measures: official enrolment of members, regulation of primaries, publicity, judicial review where appropriate, and procedures to protect members' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary voting should be subject to governmental control and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary voting ought to be regulated by government (subject to official control), with proposals such as holding primaries at registration time and subjecting nomination procedures to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider governmental oversight: official enrollment, standardized primary procedures, timing aligned with registration, and legal frameworks (example: New York primary law) to reduce fraud and party manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination reforms: direct vote, Australian ballot, petition nomination
rubrics_metrics.description: Nomination methods should be reformed—nomination by direct vote (primaries), use of the Australian ballot, and nomination by petition are recommended to reduce party bosses' control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare methods (direct vote vs convention vs certificate); promote Australian ballot for secrecy and fairness; consider petition nomination to broaden access; use examples and case law discussed in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official enrolment of party members and free party membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing official enrollment lists and ensuring party membership is freely available to all citizens help prevent abuses in primaries and ensure legal clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement registration systems for party members, safeguard enrolment procedures against fraud and 'repeating', and ensure members' rights to challenge decisions of party authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts generally decline to review internal party decisions; judicial protection of party members is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial authorities often regard party authorities' actions as final and will not review certain party contests and counts; legal protections for individual members are therefore weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing remedies for party abuses, do not rely solely on courts; pursue statutory reforms (enrollment, governmental control of primaries) and internal party protections to safeguard members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater publicity and regulation of corporate relations with parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations between corporations and political parties require greater publicity to prevent undue influence and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend transparency measures for corporate political activity and publicity requirements to expose and deter improper influence on parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere centralization or mere legal recognition of parties is insufficient—both needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions: centralization of administration without responsible parties, or legal recognition of parties without administrative centralization, will not achieve popular government and efficient administration; both reforms are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reform packages combining administrative centralization (to take technical administration out of politics) with legal and procedural party reforms (to make parties responsible and accountable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess systems comparatively—learn from English experience pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Study comparative administrative and party systems (England, Continent, U.S.) and adopt practical, experience-based reforms rather than rigidly following political theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use English examples (cabinet responsibility, municipal efficiency) as sources of practical lessons; adapt methods to local conditions rather than exact imitation of foreign models.
